sources.note: Project index checked locally for exact id tibet-1914, name Tibet, approximate lifetime 1914-1994, and the separate tibet, tibetan-empire, tibetans, proto-tibetan-cultures and tibeto-burmanese records. The lifetime is map metadata, not a verified political chronology.

sources.title: Human History Map, generated research coverage audit
sources.note: Coverage entry checked locally: tibet-1914 has no card, has six border files and six consecutive observed intervals from 1914-1920 through 1960-1994, and has no feature outside its indexed lifetime. Existing cards for medieval Tibet and the Tibetan Empire remain separate.

sources.title: Human History Map, world-1914 historical basemap topology
sources.note: Primary TopoJSON decoded locally. The tibet-1914 feature for 1914-1920 is one 162-vertex Polygon with bbox 78.4501845,27.1815913 to 98.9559896,36.5002911. Named point tests and neighboring contacts are recorded in identity.json.

sources.title: Human History Map, world-1960 historical basemap topology
sources.note: Primary TopoJSON decoded locally. The tibet-1914 feature for 1960-1994 remains one 162-vertex Polygon with nearly the same bbox and the same results for thirteen named point tests. It touches or overlaps the imported China, India, Nepal, Bhutan and Burma feature boundaries; this is display topology, not evidence of sovereignty.

sources.title: Melvyn C. Goldstein, A History of Modern Tibet, 1913-1951, University of California Press
sources.note: University-press description and contents checked. The study draws on Tibetan participants, interviews and diplomatic archives and treats the political status dispute, internal institutions, modernization arguments, the PLA invasion and Seventeen-Point Agreement. It describes competing Chinese and Tibetan historical narratives rather than endorsing either as a complete account.

sources.title: Teemu Ruskola, Suzerainty, Semi-Sovereignty, and International Legal Hierarchies on China’s Borderlands
sources.note: Peer-reviewed legal history checked for Tibet’s de facto independence, limited foreign relations and lack of general recognition as a sovereign country before 1951, plus the ambiguity of British “suzerainty” terminology. The author characterizes the 1951 outcome as annexation; that interpretation is identified, not silently converted into universal terminology.

sources.title: Karunakar Gupta, The McMahon Line 1911-45: The British Legacy, The China Quarterly
sources.note: Peer-reviewed article checked for the 1913-1914 Simla conference, Britain’s buffer-state aims, Tibetan aspirations, proposed Inner/Outer Tibet division, and the British-Tibetan relationship. It is used to expose imperial interests and unresolved status, not to validate the imported map boundary.

sources.title: Treasury of Lives, The Thirteenth Dalai Lama, Tubten Gyatso
sources.note: Scholarly biographical encyclopedia checked for the post-1912 government, army training, communication and postal systems, paper currency, Shol printing press, reform costs, resistance from senior institutions, and the limit that much of Kham and Amdo remained beyond Lhasa’s control.

sources.title: Wolfgang Bertsch, A Survey of Tibetan Paper Currency (1912-1959), Bulletin of Tibetology
sources.note: Numismatic study checked for the earliest 1913 paper notes, hand-produced printing blocks, dating clues, controlled issue, later gold backing and the 1925 Lhasa finance office. Surviving notes support object-level claims; they do not by themselves settle Tibet’s international legal status.

sources.title: Alice Travers, The Tibetan Governmental Transport and Postal System, Buddhism, Law & Society
sources.note: Peer-reviewed legal-history article checked for the reform of the older courier network, twelve Central Tibetan postal stations, the Lhasa-Gyantse route, Tibetan stamps, transfer to the British Indian system for overseas mail and the simple telegraph line. Searchable full text and article metadata were compared.

sources.title: Columbia University Libraries, online archive of the Tibet Mirror
sources.note: University special-collections announcement checked for the newspaper’s Tibetan title and transliteration, publication in Kalimpong from 1925 to 1963, circulation of world news to Tibetan readers, and the digitized issues’ 1933-1961 date range. The displayed Tibetan sample is an editorial Unicode transcription of the documented masthead title, not OCR from one page.

sources.title: Melvyn C. Goldstein, A History of Modern Tibet, 1913-1951, JSTOR open book
sources.note: Open academic book checked at the introduction and chapters 2, 18-20 for government and society, expulsion of Chinese forces after the Qing collapse, regency politics, the PLA campaign at Chamdo, negotiations and capitulation in the Seventeen-Point Agreement.

sources.title: Tibet Justice Center legal materials, Seventeen-Point Agreement (1951)
sources.note: Full English text checked for the preamble and clauses on PRC sovereignty, PLA entry, regional autonomy, the existing Tibetan political system, the Dalai and Panchen Lamas, religion, language, reforms, defense and foreign affairs. The host is a Tibetan advocacy organization, so wording was cross-checked against the PRC National People’s Congress account.

sources.title: National People’s Congress of China, How was the 17-Article Agreement signed?
sources.note: Official PRC account checked for its position that Tibetan delegates had full authority, the later telegram from the Dalai Lama’s government and Beijing’s “peaceful liberation” framing. It is treated as a participant state narrative and paired with the agreement text and independent scholarship.

sources.title: United States Office of the Historian, Foreign Relations of the United States, 1951, document 94
sources.note: Declassified diplomatic document checked for contemporary reporting that Tibet had appealed after the October 1950 invasion, received no effective UN response and faced pressure to accept PRC demands. It records US officials’ views and geopolitical interests, not a neutral transcript of Tibetan or Chinese decisions.

sources.title: Melvyn C. Goldstein, A History of Modern Tibet, Volume 2: The Estate System chapter
sources.note: University-press chapter checked for the continued Tibetan estate system during the initial 1951-1955 coexistence, its government, monastic and aristocratic estate categories, taxation and obligations, and the Chinese gradualist policy. The chapter’s social categories are not treated as a moral census of every household.

sources.title: Melvyn C. Goldstein, A History of Modern Tibet, Volume 4: In the Eye of the Storm, University of California Press
sources.note: University-press description and contents checked for the 1957-1959 buildup, March 1959 Lhasa uprising and demise of the old Tibetan political order. The book is based on Tibetan, Chinese and English documents, biographies, memoirs and specially collected interviews and challenges simplified partisan accounts.

sources.title: Spinning the Wheel: Policy Implications of the Dalai Lama’s Reincarnation, Case Western Reserve University
sources.note: Academic policy paper checked for the 10 March 1959 crowds and rumors, breakdown of negotiations, the Dalai Lama’s 17 March flight, repudiation of the agreement in exile, the end of quasi-self-rule and replacement of the old administration by the Preparatory Committee.

sources.title: Melvyn C. Goldstein, The United States, Tibet, and the Cold War
sources.note: Academic article checked for US policy toward Tibet, CIA contact with resistance leaders, training and weapons beginning in the late 1950s, the March 1959 uprising and the Dalai Lama’s exile in India. It explicitly analyzes how outside intervention may have intensified events rather than turning Tibetan actors into puppets.

sources.title: United Nations General Assembly Resolution 1353 (XIV), Question of Tibet
sources.note: Official resolution checked. Adopted in 1959, it called for respect for the Tibetan people’s fundamental human rights and distinctive cultural and religious life. It did not recognize Tibet as an independent state or draw a border, limits made explicit in the card.

sources.title: State Council of China, Successful Practice of Regional Ethnic Autonomy in Tibet
sources.note: Official PRC white paper checked for the Preparatory Committee, dismissal of the old government after the 1959 uprising, land and political reforms, and the 1 September 1965 founding of the Tibet Autonomous Region. Its “peaceful liberation,” “rebellion” and emancipation language is presented as the PRC’s state framing, not neutral vocabulary.

sources.title: Melvyn Goldstein, Ben Jiao and Tanzen Lhundrup, On the Cultural Revolution in Tibet, University of California Press
sources.note: University-press study checked for the Cultural Revolution’s factional conflicts, local Tibetan participation, the 1969 Nyemo violence and the authors’ warning that not every conflict was simply an ethnic-nationalist revolt. It is paired with oral-history evidence about coercion and deprivation.

sources.title: National Security Archive, US diplomatic reporting on Tibetan liberalization in the early 1980s
sources.note: George Washington University archive checked for declassified cables on Hu Yaobang’s 1980 visit, economic and cultural policy changes, renewed family travel, monastery restoration, education, persistent poverty, Chinese-language advantages and the limits of the religious revival. Diplomatic observers and interviewees had their own perspectives.

sources.title: United Nations Commission on Human Rights, Situation in Tibet, E/CN.4/1992/37
sources.note: UN-hosted report checked for demonstrations beginning in 1987, killings and detentions reported by non-governmental sources, the 8 March 1989 imposition of martial law and its stated official justification, and the May 1990 lifting. Contested casualty estimates are not repeated as settled totals.

sources.title: Case Western Reserve University Center for Research on Tibet, Tibetan History, Society and Marriage
sources.note: University research portal checked for the published Goldstein-Miller debate over Tibetan dependency and command, plus academic works on taxation, social structure, marriage and polyandry. It demonstrates an active scholarly argument and supports caution about reducing society to one slogan.

sources.title: Melvyn C. Goldstein, Serfdom and Mobility in Traditional Tibetan Society, Journal of Asian Studies
sources.note: Peer-reviewed 1971 study checked for hereditary ties to estates, government/monastic/aristocratic lords, differing dependent categories and channels of personal mobility. Its terminology and refugee-interview method have been debated, so the card attributes the analytical label rather than presenting propaganda from either side.

sources.title: Melvyn C. Goldstein, Stratification, Polyandry, and Family Structure in Central Tibet
sources.note: Peer-reviewed anthropological study checked for the relationship among landholding, household continuity and fraternal polyandry in Central Tibet. It documents one important pattern alongside monogamy and other arrangements and cannot be generalized to every class, locality or Tibetan-speaking region.

sources.title: Library of Congress, Tibetan Oral History Archive Project
sources.note: Official collection guide checked for almost 700 interviews, including over 600 common-folk interviews and separate political and Drepung monastery collections covering traditional and socialist eras through the Cultural Revolution. Oral testimony is memory evidence with individual scope, not an automatic fact for everyone.

sources.title: UNHCR, The State of the World’s Refugees 2000: The Tibetan refugee community in India
sources.note: UNHCR retrospective checked at chapter 3, box 3.1, for the Dalai Lama’s 1959 flight, Tibetan refugee settlements across India, and India’s policy of allowing the community to maintain a distinct identity, cultural life and political-administrative system. Published after the atlas endpoint, it is used only to establish continuity through and beyond 1994, not conditions inside Tibet.

sources.title: Tibet Oral History Project, Interview 74 with Tsering Wangmo
sources.note: Translated 2007 interview checked at transcript pages 3-6. Wangmo, born in 1920 in U-Tsang, recalled one pastoral household’s relatives, livestock, children’s work, dairy and wool labor, tsampa and soup, clothing, songs, weddings, river water, winter ice and bathing. Retrospective personal testimony is not treated as a survey.

sources.title: Library of Congress, Common Folk Oral History interview OR.0007.01 with Phurbu Chogba
sources.note: Translated interview checked at transcript pages 1-6. Phurbu Chogba, born in 1949, recalled family flight from estate obligations, childhood service and beating, post-1959 village school, Tibetan reading and mathematics, activist work, a difficult hospital journey, commune-era shortages and later decollectivization. It is one life, not a representative statistic.

sources.title: Library of Congress catalog record, oral history interview of Phurbu
sources.note: Official catalog record and linked transcript checked for Phurbu Chogba’s background, post-reform Social School and oral-history files. The linked transcript pages 1-2 record villagers carrying an appendicitis patient to county and prefectural hospitals for surgery and a blood transfusion.

sources.title: Tibet Oral History Project, interview 209 with Lobsang Thardho
sources.note: Interview catalog and linked transcript checked for Lobsang Thardho’s recollection of beginning lessons around age five or six at the Potala with his opera-singer uncle, entering Ganden monastery at thirteen, and describing monastic study and routine. It is one comparatively privileged educational path, not evidence that all children attended school.

sources.title: Library of Congress, Political History interview H.0001.14
sources.note: Translated former-official interview checked at transcript pages 2-4. The interviewee recalled Lhasa toilets receiving ash to reduce odor, composted toilet material used as fertilizer, different PLA vegetable-fertilizing practice, imported rice and 1950s food markets. The memory is specific to Lhasa and should not be universalized.

sources.title: Tibetan medicine: a unique heritage of person-centered medicine, EPMA Journal
sources.note: Peer-reviewed medical-history overview checked for the 13th Dalai Lama’s 1916 foundation of a Lhasa clinic, school and pharmacy, Tibetan diagnostic theory, compound medicines and later institutional continuity. Historical practices are described as practices, not endorsed as effective modern treatment.

sources.title: State Council Information Office of China, Democratic Reform in Tibet: Sixty Years On
sources.note: Official PRC white paper checked for reported 1958-1965 changes in roads, schools, medical institutions, hospital beds and health workers. These are state administrative counts and achievement claims; the card uses them to document institution building while explicitly noting they do not measure quality, coercion or equal access.

sources.title: Tibet Heritage Fund, The Old City of Lhasa: Water and Sanitation Project
sources.note: Conservation project report checked for a 1997 old-city study, just after the atlas endpoint: vulnerable toilets in traditional buildings, water pressure, hand-emptied cesspits in some circa-1990 housing, drains and a new sewer connection. It is used to define a late evidence limit, not projected backward onto all earlier homes.

sources.title: PRC Embassy, Tibetan Education: Difficulties and Recovery (1966-1986)
sources.note: Official PRC education history checked for the 1980 policy conference, primary-school expansion, teacher training, Tibetan-language textbooks and courses, subsidies and official acknowledgement of continuing problems. Its success framing and figures are treated as government claims, not independent outcome measures.

sources.title: Case Western Reserve University, Voices from Tibet
sources.note: University feature checked for Goldstein and Beall’s 1980s field observations of Changtang pastoralists after commune policies were reversed: household livestock returned, religious restrictions eased, and prayer flags, yak-hair tents, herding and traditional dress remained visible. It is a fieldwork account, not proof that nothing had changed.

sources.title: Library of Congress, name authority decision for Tibet and Tibet Autonomous Region
sources.note: Official cataloging decision checked for separate jurisdiction headings: Tibet for the jurisdiction before 1 September 1965 and Tibet Autonomous Region (China) for the province-level jurisdiction formalized on that date. Catalog headings clarify identity; they are not a ruling on historical sovereignty.

proposedOverrides.name: Tibet (1914-1994 atlas record)
proposedOverrides.summary: An approximate regional atlas record spanning de facto Tibetan self-government, PRC incorporation, socialist transformation, cultural destruction, revival and dissent; its nearly unchanged polygon is not one continuous sovereignty claim.

batchIdentityNotes.finding: Exact target is the approximate 1914-1994 historical-basemap record. It is separate from the already-carded tibet (1000-1783) and tibetan-empire records and from prehistoric or ethnolinguistic umbrella IDs.

Six consecutive target features cover 1914-1920, 1920-1930, 1930-1938, 1938-1945, 1945-1960 and 1960-1994. Every one is a single polygon; the outline and named point-test results remain nearly unchanged despite fundamental political change.

All six features include tested Lhasa, Shigatse, Gyantse, Tsetang, Nagqu, Chamdo and Gartok and exclude tested Leh, Xining, Lanzhou, Chengdu, Kathmandu and Thimphu. These are display-geometry tests only, not historical control or sovereignty findings.

The atlas ID crosses the 1950 PLA campaign, 1951 agreement, 1959 institutional rupture and 1965 Tibet Autonomous Region founding. The narrative does not treat it as one continuous sovereign state, and the 1994 endpoint is a catalog cutoff rather than a fall.
